1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 842 kWh (62,601 − 61,759), line items sum to $159.43 ($18.75 + $28.59 + $112.09), and the change versus last month is +$7.97 ($159.43 − $151.46); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map each billing period to its AEP Ohio tariff by date: last month (2026-03-08 to 2026-04-07) falls entirely under the pre-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.38; tier-1 variable $0.0263125 + $0.13441 = $0.1607225/kWh). The current period (2026-04-07 to 2026-05-08) straddles the 2026-04-10 change, so prorate the fixed charge ($18.38 vs $18.788) and blend the tier-1 variable rate ($0.1607225 vs $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh) across the boundary; note the periods differ in length (30 vs 31 days).

3. Compute days_usd from the one extra billing day valued at the baseline daily fixed-charge equivalent (do not automatically set to zero, unlike same-length prior periods).

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 16.5 / HDD 422.5) to current (CDD 42 / HDD 249), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Compute price_usd from the tariff changes (higher fixed charge and higher blended variable rate) applied to baseline usage, compute usage_usd from the 14 kWh increase (828 → 842) valued at the effective rate, then set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly +$7.97.

6. Check for a billing error by comparing the tariff-modeled current-period total to the actual $159.43; if the difference exceeds rounding, set billing_error_suspected = true and billing_error_usd to the discrepancy, otherwise false and null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
